options: A type of index fragmentation
A SQL Server feature for automatically syncing environments
The gap between what source control says a schema should be and what the live database actually looks like
The natural growth of a transaction log over time
questions.explain: Drift is the mismatch between the source-of-truth (source control) and the live, actual state of the database.

questions.q: Which scenario, from this lesson, is a typical, mundane cause of schema drift?
options: A scheduled backup job running on time
An index added directly in production during an incident that never gets backported to source control
A DACPAC deployment completing successfully
A stored procedure being called by an application
questions.explain: Drift usually starts with an ordinary out-of-process change — like an emergency production fix — that never makes it back into source control.

questions.q: Why is drift particularly dangerous during a DACPAC-based deployment?
options: Drift only affects manual scripted deployments, never DACPACs
The deployment tool trusts that the live database matches what it expects, so drift can cause the diff to fail or silently undo an undocumented fix
DACPACs cannot be used once drift exists, permanently
DACPAC deployments are immune to drift by design
questions.explain: A DACPAC's generated diff assumes the live database matches its expected starting state; drift breaks that assumption and can cause failures or unintended reversions.

questions.q: What is the practical way to detect schema drift before it causes a deployment failure, per this lesson?
options: Restore from backup weekly regardless of need
Disable all indexes to prevent drift from occurring
Run a recurring schema-compare between a source-control snapshot (e.g., a DACPAC) and the live database, not just at deployment time
Wait for a deployment to fail and investigate afterward
questions.explain: SSDT's schema-compare tooling, run as a recurring check, catches drift while it's still small instead of at deployment time.

questions.q: According to this lesson, is schema drift primarily a technical problem or a process problem?
options: Purely a technical problem solved entirely by better deployment tooling
A hardware issue related to disk latency
A process problem — the real fix is closing the gap that let out-of-process changes happen in the first place
An inevitability that cannot be reduced by any process change
questions.explain: Detecting drift with schema-compare helps, but the real fix is a process rule that no live change ships without a matching source-control update.
